item.title: Victoria continues regional neighbourhood battery rollout
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: The Victorian government has officially opened a neighbourhood battery in the regional city of Marysville, as part of its $42 million 100 Neighbourhood Battery Program.
item.content:encoded:
The Victoria state government has officially opened a neighbourhood battery in the regional city of Marysville, approximately 100 kilometres northeast of Melbourne, as part of its $42 million (USD 29.4 million) 100 Neighbourhood Battery Program.

In partnership with the local government Murrindindi Shire Council, the Central Victorian Greenhouse Alliance and the Goulburn Murray Climate Alliance, the Marysville Community Centre site features a 59 kW / 224 kWh neighbourhood battery energy storage system (BESS) paired with an existing rooftop solar system.

Marysville is one of 11 communities benefiting from the Central Victorian Greenhouse Alliance’s Powering Resilience in the Regions project, backed by the 100 Neighbourhood Batteries program.

The Powering Resilience in the Regions project has also installed batteries at council-owned facilities in Pomonal, Trentham, Newborough, Churchill, Bonnie Doon, Castlemaine, Korumburra, Benalla, Bright and Wendouree.

These facilities will also provide places for residents to access power and support when power supply is disrupted.

On Phillip Island, Mondo Power has partnered with Bass Coast Shire Council and Totally Renewable Phillip Island to install seven neighbourhood batteries on council-managed land.

A share of the batteries’ annual operating income will support local community initiatives.

Labor is delivering 139 neighbourhood batteries across 60 council areas, with 80 already installed with a combined storage capacity of 23,000 kWh.

Victoria Minister for Energy and Resources Jaclyn Symes said the batteries mean lower bills for community facilities and more reliable power for locals.

“Marysville Community Centre brings people together – and spending less on power means more money for the services and activities locals rely on.”

item.title: 350 GWh Snowy 2.0 project cost update now peaks at $25 billion
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Snow Hydro has released an update on costs and a delivery schedule for the 2.2 GW Snowy 2.0 pumped hydroelectric project, assessing completion cost of the job to commissioning in 2029 falls between $22.5 and $25 billion.
item.content:encoded:
A new update from principal Snowy 2.0 contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV) on the costs and a delivery schedule for the 2.2 GW / 350,000 MWh Snowy 2.0 pumped-storage hydroelectricity megaproject, has reassessed completion of the job to commissioning in 2029 to land between $22.5 and $25 billion (USD 15.7 and 17.5 billion).

At the project’s first announcement in early 2017 the cost was estimated to be $2 billion, revised later that year to between $3.8 and $4.5 billion, then $6.1 billion in 2018, and $12 billion in 2023.

The cost reassessment is place squarely on FGJV’s underestimation of the delivery scope, including cost and planning underperformance, the contractor’s inability to meet productivity targets due to construction complexities, a revamp of the design involving a detailed technical analysis, and external factors such as global cost escalation for equipment, services and people exceeding allowances made at a 2023 contract reset.

Snowy Hydro Chief Executive Officer Dennis Barnes said the cost increase is disappointing, but as the project is now not on a fixed price contract, it is protected from the ‘weight of billions of dollars in claims from the contractor’, which it previously was.

With more than 5,000 people working on the project, the 2023 contract reset included mechanisms to support FGJVs cost and program management, including directing FGJV to establish a project control office with enhanced data and analytics to drive productivity and identify emerging risks early, which is now operational.

“Like the original Snowy Scheme, which still underpins energy reliability more than 70 years on, Snowy 2.0 is a generational investment in our energy sovereignty and a national asset owned by all Australians,” Barnes said.

“Snowy 2.0’s massive, long-duration storage will be the grid’s insurance policy against multi-day wind and solar droughts, helping to prevent blackouts and control price spikes that would otherwise flow through to household electricity bills.”

Progress

Regarded as Australia’s largest energy security project, the Snowy Hydro scheme expansion project will provide long-duration energy storage equivalent to approximately 26 million home batteries, or enough to power 3 million homes for a week.

The project is transitioning from extensive cavern excavation and machine tunnelling, which are  90% and 65% complete, respectively, to the physical assembly and fit-out of the very large-scale underground power station.

All six reversible turbines, manufactured by Germany-headquartered hydropower engineering company Voith Hydro, with bespoke components fabricated at Voith’s production facility in Shanghai, China, have arrived in Australia.

With a lifespan estimated at 150 years or lasting until 2176, the underground powerhouse complex is a cavern network located a kilometre underground, which Snowy Hydro said is comparable in scale to the Sydney Opera House.

A next phase includes crews preparing to position massive inlet valves and spiral casings, alongside high-voltage transformers weighing over 400 tonnes each, and a multitude of hydropower components.

item.title: Solar drives all-time generation peak of 80.4% in September quarter
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Solar generation was the primary driver of a renewable and storage generation all-time peak contribution of 80.4% of total NEM generation on 19 September 2026, with distributed solar supplying 51.8% of total generation at the time, and grid-scale solar adding a further 16.4%.
item.content:encoded:
Solar generation was the primary driver of an all-time 80.4% peak in the National Electricity Market (NEM) from renewable and storage generation in the half hour to 1230 on Saturday, 19 September 2026.

This was 3.2 pp higher than the same period in 2025, and exceeded a previous record set in October 2025, by 1.8 pp. At the time of the Q3 2026 peak, distributed solar supplied 51.8% of total generation, and grid-scale solar adding a further 16.4%.

Also, during Q3 2026, distributed solar capacity across the NEM reached 27 GW from 3.9 million consumer energy resources (CER) installations, representing a year-on-year increase of 12%, which drove output to a Q3 average high of 3,203 MW (+13%), and setting a new peak generation record of 16,992 MW on 20 September 2026.

“CER solar capacity expanded consistently across all regions, with New South Wales (NSW) reaching 9.3 GW, followed by Queensland at 8.3 GW,” the data source and Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) Quarterly Dynamic Report (QDR) says.

“Victoria and South Australia distributed PV capacity reached 6.1 GW and 3.1 GW respectively. Growth in Tasmania remained comparatively smaller and reached 0.4 GW.”

AEMO Executive General Manager Policy and Corporate Affairs Violette Mouchaileh said the quarter showed how demand, supply and storage were continuing to change across the NEM.

“Electricity use continues to grow, but more solar and storage is changing when energy is produced, drawn from the grid and shifted across the day,” Mouchaileh said.

Grid-scale solar generation saw significant growth in Q3 2026, jumping 512 MW (+30%) year-on-year to reach a new Q3 high average of 2,211 MW, that boosted total generation share by 1.9 pp to 8.5%, and achieved an all-time peak output of 8,290 MW in the interval 30 minutes ending 1500 on 27 August 2026, which is 112 MW above the previous peak set in Q1 2026, or up 1.4%.

Network Curtailment

“ Total network curtailment of wind and solar generation reached a new Q3 high, averaging 281 MW, up 139 MW year-on-year,” the QDR says.

“Grid-scale solar accounted for most of this increase, with curtailment rising by 105 MW, to average 169 MW this quarter. As a percentage of solar availability, curtailment increased by 3.6 pp year-on-year to 6.7%.”

“Increases were greatest in NSW with curtailment at 104 MW (+64 MW), primarily at facilities in the south of the state, followed by Queensland at 48 MW (+41 MW) concentrated at facilities in the north of the state (Figure 51). In Victoria and South Australia, grid-scale solar curtailment remained largely unchanged year-on-year, averaging 15 MW and 1.0 MW respectively,” the report says.

Batteries

Supported by the uptake of home batteries via the federal government’s Cheaper Home Battery Program (CHBP), 75% of households with rooftop solar and batteries installed, drew less power from the grid during the evening peak between 1600 to 2100, in Q3 2026.

The cumulative CER battery capacity under the program reached 13,917 MWh in Q3 2026 and installations grew from 420,266 to 482,835 between 1 July 2026 to 30 September 2026, an increase of 62,569 battery installations in the quarter.

“Relative to the end of Q2 2026, cumulative CER battery capacity across the NEM increased by 1,652 MWh (+13%), with more than 10% growth in every region by the end of Q3 2026. Under the program, New South Wales recorded 5,885 MWh of installed capacity, followed by Victoria at 3,185 MWh and Queensland at 3,166 MWh. South Australia and Tasmania reached 1,568 MWh and 114 MWh, respectively,” the report says.

Mouchaileh said batteries continue to shift record amounts of renewable energy into the higher-demand evening period, when households and businesses typically need more power.

“Increased battery charging and discharging contributed to significantly lower evening peak prices, with batteries setting prices in almost half of dispatch intervals, up from 18% a year ago,” Mouchaileh said.

Energy shifted by grid-scale batteries more than tripled year-on-year, with batteries charging 13.4 GWh of energy per day on average during daylight hours before discharging 10.9 GWh during the evening peak,  when they supplied 8% of total generation, exceeding gas-fired generation (5.1%) for the first time in any quarter.

item.title: No roof left behind: how advanced solar technology can bring difficult commercial buildings into Australia’s energy transition
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: A new 1.3 MW rooftop system at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre shows what is possible when advanced module technology meets site-specific engineering. Installed across a curved, partially shaded roof, it is about 53% larger than the 850 kW tender – and around 60% larger than a conventional, shade-avoiding design would have allowed.
item.content:encoded:
The clean-energy transition can’t stop at the easy roofs

Australia has installed around 22 GW of rooftop solar on homes but only about 5.6 GW on commercial and industrial (C&I) buildings – even though businesses use more electricity than households, and use much of it during daylight hours when solar is generating.

The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) estimates the technical rooftop potential across C&I buildings at close to 40 GW, rising above 80 GW when agricultural buildings are included. Yet forecasts suggest the sector may reach only 17–31 GW by 2050.

Policy, tariffs, connection processes and finance all contribute to that gap. But another barrier gets far less attention: many commercial roofs are curved, shaded, structurally constrained or architecturally sensitive.

These buildings shouldn’t be left out of Australia’s energy transition – they need a different design approach.

The easy-roof economy

The commercial solar market has good reasons to favour simple roofs. A flat or low-pitch metal roof with clear access, minimal shading and spare structural capacity can often be designed from an established template, using standard mounting systems and predictable installation methods. Engineering risk is low and margins are easy to protect.

Complex roofs are rarely rejected outright. More often, they are designed down: the array is confined to the clear, unshaded section, and curved, shaded or load-limited areas are excluded. The project may be technically sound, but it is materially smaller than the site could support.

For businesses, solar is a significant capital investment, and a system sized well below daytime demand leaves the site exposed to grid prices for the next 25–30 years. As business capital and public incentives flow into the C&I segment, design decisions like these will determine how much each project returns – and how much of the sector’s 40 GW potential is ever realised.

A different design pathway

The Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre (MSAC) shows how a complex roof can be approached differently.

The venue’s roof is curved and partially shaded by surrounding towers and cables. Structural and aesthetic requirements also limited the suitability of conventional tilted mounting, and a tilted system would have needed wider row spacing to manage inter-row shading, further reducing the usable area. Under a conventional design approach, the project was expected to deliver around 800–850 kW.

Melbourne EPC Next Green Group took a different path, designing around the building’s structural and architectural requirements rather than a standard template.

Power density

The team selected AIKO Comet All Back Contact (ABC) mono-glass modules to maximise generation from the usable roof area. With all electrical contacts moved to the rear of the cell, the front surface has no busbars or grid lines to block light, lifting power density per square metre. On a roof where usable area is the binding constraint, more watts per module means more kilowatts on the same footprint.

Weight

The Comet single-glass modules weigh 28 kg each, giving a high power-to-weight ratio. That mattered: the installation placed 2,016 modules and four kilometres of rail – more than 56 tonnes of equipment – on a steep, curved roof, so every kilogram per module counted against the structure’s limits.

Shade tolerance

In conventional modules, cells are wired in series and grouped behind bypass diodes, typically three per module. A single shaded cell can switch out a whole cell group – about a third of the module – and cause further mismatch losses along the string, while shaded cells that aren’t bypassed can develop hot-spots. That is why designers generally leave shaded roof areas empty.

AIKO’s ABC modules manage shading at the level of individual cells. TÜV NORD testing found they produced up to 30% more electricity than TOPCon modules with a single cell fully shaded, and in separate TÜV NORD hot-spot testing, shaded ABC cells stabilised below 100°C compared with around 170°C for TOPCon. The modules also hold TÜV Rheinland Class A certification for partial-shading resistance. For NGG, that meant the shaded parts of the roof could be designed as generating area.

These characteristics don’t eliminate the roof’s constraints. But they improve the economics of using areas where shading is unavoidable, and give the EPC more design flexibility to use more of the roof and pursue a larger system.

From flexibility to a buildable design

Next Green Group turned that advantage into a buildable design. The team ran a trial installation on the roof’s sharpest curves and completed wind and dead-load testing before full installation. Because tilted racking would have cut across the curved roofline, it installed a flush-mount system that follows the curve – preserving the building’s profile and increasing panel density, since flush-mounted panels don’t need the gaps left between tilted rows.

Flush mounting has a thermal trade-off: with less airflow behind the modules, arrays run hotter, and output falls as cell temperature rises. In independent CEA testing, AIKO’s ABC modules recorded a Pmax temperature coefficient of –0.26%/°C, compared with around –0.29%/°C typical of TOPCon – a difference that applies to every hour of generation over the system’s life.

The completed 1.3 MW array is about 500 kW larger than the roughly 800 kW a conventional, shade-avoiding layout would have allowed – around 60% more capacity from the same roof.

“A complex roof does not necessarily have low solar potential. In many cases, it needs a more site-specific engineering response, paired with modules that can improve the capacity, weight and shading trade-offs.” – Nathaniel Galindo, Executive General Manager – Integrated Energy Solutions, Next Green Group

Generation where the load is

The additional capacity serves MSAC’s energy-intensive daytime load: pools, water treatment, heating and cooling, ventilation, lighting, courts and scoreboards.

The system is expected to generate more than 1 GWh of renewable electricity a year – equivalent to about 254 homes – meeting around one-quarter of the venue’s electricity needs and saving an estimated $70,000 (USD 49,129) a year, according to the Victorian Government.

The SEC owns and operates the system under an agreement with the State Sport Centres Trust. That gives the project a broader public-interest dimension: a higher-capacity rooftop system creates greater value for a major community venue, not just for an individual building owner.

The project also marks a practical shift in how MSAC manages energy. A room beside the main switchboard that once housed a 20-year-old gas cogeneration unit now holds nine 110 kW GoodWe HT Series inverters and the PV distribution board – existing infrastructure repurposed for on-site renewable generation.

Beyond the easy roofs

MSAC is a case study in how detailed engineering and advanced solar technology can overcome roof constraints to deliver materially larger, more valuable solar systems.

For commercial rooftops, the question isn’t simply whether solar can fit. It’s whether the system has been designed to get the full value from the available roof space.

“Many of Australia’s most energy-intensive community and commercial assets have complex roofs. Our aim is to make solar more accessible to these sites, so they can benefit from clean energy rather than being left behind because a conventional design cannot fully respond to their constraints.” – Thomas Bywater, Head of AIKO Australia and New Zealand

Australia’s energy transition won’t be complete if businesses miss out on the benefits of clean energy because their roofs have constraints.

Nor will the full value of the C&I market be realised if systems are designed around what is quickest and most profitable to sell and install, rather than the building’s energy needs and the full potential of its roof.

item.title: China proposes ban on exports of perovskite, tandem solar manufacturing technology
item.dc:creator: Vincent Shaw
item.description: China has proposed banning exports of selected high-efficiency perovskite and tandem solar manufacturing technologies, alongside new restrictions on advanced polysilicon, wafer and crystalline-silicon cell production processes. The proposed measures would cover 12 photovoltaic technologies, with public consultation open until 15 November 2026.
item.content:encoded:
China’s Ministry of Commerce (Mofcom) and Ministry of Science and Technology have proposed prohibiting exports of selected high-efficiency perovskite and tandem solar manufacturing technologies, alongside new restrictions on advanced polysilicon, wafer and crystalline-silicon cell production know-how.

The proposals, published on 16 October 2026 under Joint Announcement No. 48 of 2026, would add 12 photovoltaic technologies to China’s Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export.

They are part of a broader consultation covering 40 technologies across sectors including solar energy, artificial intelligence and biomedicine. The public consultation runs until 15 November 2026.

The proposed export bans cover production processes and related equipment manufacturing technologies for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells based on wafers measuring at least 182 mm and achieving conversion efficiencies of 30% or higher. They also include slot-die coating processes for perovskites with coating widths of at least 1.1 metres.

Additional thresholds apply to large-area modules, including single-junction perovskite modules measuring at least 1 square metre with conversion efficiencies of 18% or higher, and perovskite tandem modules of the same minimum area with efficiencies of at least 28%.

The proposed controls target manufacturing technologies meeting these specifications rather than exports of finished modules.

Other technologies proposed for prohibition include cold-hydrogenation fluidised-bed processes for trichlorosilane production with annual single-line capacities of at least 250,000 metric tons, and silane-based fluidized-bed processes with annual capacities of at least 20,000 metric tons.

The draft also covers processes for manufacturing silicon wafers no thicker than 70 micrometres and certain edge-passivation technologies for thin crystalline-silicon cells, along with related equipment manufacturing know-how.

The proposed restricted-export category includes polysilicon plant engineering technologies for production lines with annual capacities of at least 30,000 metric tons, as well as advanced crystal-pulling and wafer-cutting processes.

It also covers specified high-performance manufacturing processes for tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon), back-contact (BC) and heterojunction (HJT) solar cells, including deposition, passivation, diffusion and metallisation technologies.

The HJT provisions include certain p-type technologies evaluated under air mass zero (AM0) illumination conditions relevant to space applications.

Under China’s technology import and export regulations, prohibited technologies cannot be exported, while restricted technologies can be transferred overseas only with government approval and the necessary licenses.

The proposed export bans and licensing requirements have not yet taken effect. However, a separate interim registration requirement took effect on 16 October 2026 when the announcement was issued.

Companies must register planned exports of the listed technologies, including qualifying key equipment, through the Mofcom’s online system before transfer.

The requirement covers intellectual property transfers, overseas technology licensing, changes in ownership or control involving foreign entities, and transactions that are underway but have not yet been completed.

The Mofcom said the proposals address national security concerns as photovoltaic technologies increasingly find applications in aerospace, defense and other sensitive sectors.

The ministry said technologies that fall below the specified thresholds, as well as finished products manufactured using controlled technologies, are outside the proposed scope. It added that the measures do not target any particular country, region or company.

If adopted, the controls could reinforce China’s position in advanced PV manufacturing by limiting overseas access to some of its most sophisticated production technologies.

Although exports of finished solar cells and modules would not be directly affected, transfers of controlled manufacturing know-how through technology licensing, overseas production-line installation and commissioning, equipment exports and on-site technical support could be prohibited or subject to government approval.

In the near term, the measures could delay overseas PV manufacturing projects, increase compliance costs and limit the deployment of advanced Chinese production technologies abroad.

Over the longer term, the restrictions could strengthen China’s influence over the international diffusion of next-generation PV manufacturing technologies, potentially slowing efforts by overseas manufacturers to close the technological gap.

However, tighter controls could also complicate Chinese manufacturers’ international expansion plans and heighten trade tensions or prompt retaliatory measures.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: 80.9 GW quarterly pipeline of clean energy projects surpasses current 77 GW capacity
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: For the first time, the pipeline of clean energy generation and storage projects progressing through the National Electricity Market connection process, equal to a combined capacity of 80.9 GW, surpasses current capacity of 77 GW.
item.content:encoded:
The Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMOs) September quarter Connections Scorecard shows the pipeline of clean energy generation and storage projects, at 80.9 GW, has surpassed existing capacity (77 GW), for the first time.

Leading the way are battery energy storage systems (BESS), which account for over half of capacity in the end-to-end connection process from application to commissioning, at 55%.

Hybrid solar and battery projects at 19% then lead wind (15%), standalone solar (5%), hydro (5%) and gas (1%).

AEMO received 25 new connection applications totalling 7.5 GW during the quarter, with 19 battery projects accounting for 5.8 GW, or 76% of new capacity seeking connection.

The Scorecard shows 23 projects totalling 4.5 GW received application approval, including 17 batteries (3.6 GW), four solar hybrid (0.4 GW), and one solar (0.3 GW).

Four battery projects were registered in the quarter, and connected to the National Electricity Market (NEM), with total discharge capacity of 1 GW and storage capacity of 3.4 GWh.

Six connection projects and one alteration reached full output this quarter, including three BESS in Victoria with a combined capacity of 0.8 GW / 1.3 GWh, and one 0.25 GW / 0.5 GWh BESS, two solar projects totalling 225 MW, and an existing battery added 180 MW capacity, with total combined full output reaching 1.3 GW.

AEMO Group Manager Onboarding & Connections James Lindley said together with more battery projects there is also an increase in the number of longer-duration storage.

“[This includes] nearly 40% of battery projects that can provide between three and 10 hours of storage. This can enhance energy resilience when renewable generation output is low,” Lindley said.

Total capacity by connection stage shows that 88% of the pipeline remains in the early application and proponent implementation stages, with capacity growing 101% to 38.5 GW and 42% to 32.3 GW, respectively.

Lindley said it is critical for electricity reliability that projects continue advancing to commissioning in the lead up to 15 GW of generation being scheduled to retire in the coming decade and electricity consumption forecast to increase by more than 40%.

“The figures demonstrate strong investor interest in new energy infrastructure, while highlighting the importance of progressing viable projects through to commissioning,” Lindley said.

To help streamline registration processes, enhance technical frameworks and improve transparency and predictability of connection outcomes, AEMO and the industry are progressing initiatives such as the Connections Reform Initiative Phase 2.

item.title: Ampt string optimiser technology chosen for Victoria hybrid solar and battery project
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: DC optimiser provider Ampt been selected for a new 8.2 MWdc / 20 MWh mid-scale solar-plus-storage project in Victoria.
item.content:encoded:
United States-headquartered DC optimiser provider Ampt been selected for a new 8.2 MWdc / 20 MWh mid-scale solar-plus-storage project in Victoria.

The 8.2 MWdc of solar generation is paired with 4.95 MW of power conversion capacity and 20 MWh of battery storage.

Ampt’s string optimiser technology will connect the solar array directly to a shared DC bus between the battery and battery inverter contributing to lower upfront costs by eliminating the need for central DC/DC converters, solar inverters, or transformers.

The direct-to-battery (D2B) architecture helps increase production along with revenue by mitigating losses due to electrical mismatch caused by module degradation and other sources of imbalance such as temperature, shade, and soiling.

Ampt Australia Country Director Russell French said by deploying distribution-connected mid-scale systems directly into the existing local grid, close to where power is consumed, developers add renewable energy capacity while reducing the need for costly infrastructure upgrades.

“When battery storage is co-located with mid-scale solar, these hybrid systems can capture excess daytime generation and dispatch it during the evening peak, helping stabilise the local network rather than overloading it,” French said.

The D2B architecture also enables the fast grid response that contingency frequency control ancillary services (FCAS) markets require.

With 4.95 MW of inverter capacity, the Victoria project is the “missing middle” type of hybrid solar and battery project up to 5 MW that the $100 million (USD 70.2 million) Clean Energy Finance Corporation (CEFC) commitment to the Distribution Connected Accelerator Program (DCAP), is designed to advance.

item.title: SAJ all-in-one home energy system receives CEC approval
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Chinese smart energy solutions company SAJ has received Clean Energy Council approval for it's EK70 HS5 and EK90 HS5 all-in-one energy solution.
item.content:encoded:
China-headquartered smart energy solutions company SAJ has received Clean Energy Council (CEC) approval for it’s EK70 HS5 and EK90 HS5 all-in-one energy solution.

The CEC certification makes SAJ the first brand to be listed under the SA TS 5398:2025 Australian technical specification for electrical energy storage (EES) equipment safety.

The EK70 combines hybrid inverter, LFP battery and whole-home backup in one unit, utilitising modular 6, 7 and 9 kWh battery block stacks to suit household sizing. Modules use blind-mate connectors, no complex external cabling, wireless-pro meter, providing longer range, more stable connectivity, and wiring-free installation.

The EK90 provides a premium tier, with 12,000 cycles, a nine-layer safety protection, edge artificial intelligence (AI) and a 15-year warranty.

CEC certificates for the EK70 and EK90 HS5s will be formally presented to SAJ during All Energy Australia, 28 October, 2pm, Stand M143.

SAJ Electric Australia Sales Director Alan Li said All Energy is where the industry sees what’s next, and for SAJ that’s the EK70 HS5 and EK90 HS5.

“Installers told us they want one integrated system that’s faster to install and that they can stand behind. Being the first brand listed under SA TS 5398 is the proof,” Li said.

The company will also be signing a strategic cooperation agreement covering safety, quality and compliance, with global solar testing and certification body DEKRA.

Other products being exhibited during All Energy will be the B2S and H2 modular storage, along with the latest in SAJ’s residential range and the AI-assisted energy management app elekeeper 5.0, which offers a five-minute app commissioning and remote diagnosis service.

Commercial and industrial (C&I) solutions will also be on display.

item.title: S-5! challenges metal roof off-purlin solar mounting assumptions
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: S-5! is challenging assumptions about metal roof off-purlin solar mounting in a new white paper it says conclusively demonstrates metal roof panels possess the structural capacity for mounting solar between purlins.
item.content:encoded:
A new United States-headquartered metal roof engineering company S-5! white paper challenges the assumption solar attachment points must be directly located over purlins to ensure structural adequacy.

The ‘Solar Mounting Off Purlin on Metal Roof Sheeting’ technical paper investigates the assumption via laboratory testing for Australian building codes and standards and documented field performance.

The paper presents evidence that metal roof sheeting can reliably support solar attachments between purlins when systems are property engineered and installed.

Wind uplift resistance, load distribution and the structural role of roof panels are all examined in the paper, supported by static and cyclic load testing results, full-assembly testing and examples of solar installations that have withstood extreme hurricane conditions.

The paper points to utilising proper load distribution and not just proximity to structural purlins as key to evaluating the complete load path, including roof sheeting, solar fixings, and supporting structure.

“Metal roofs come in two distinct styles, each with a different method of attachment: standing seam (or concealed-fix), and exposed-fastened (exposed-fix). In both roof types, the seams or ribs that run from the eave to the ridge act as structural elements,” the paper says.

The paper’s findings support the integrity of S-5!‘s PVKIT 3.0 rail-less solar mounting system and Facet Mount.

“Clamps or brackets are attached to the seams or ribs with an interface called the PVKIT® to secure the PV module frames, eliminating the need for rails. The clamps and brackets can be attached anywhere along the seams or ribs, as well as directly over the purlins,” the paper explains.

The PVKIT 3.0 is available in standard and optional integrated 50 mm riser configurations, providing additional space for wire routing, module-level power electronics and other balance of system components.

The S-5! high-pressure cast aluminium Facet Mount offers 16 fastening locations designed for flexibility and increased load distribution while preserving single-ply membrance roof integrity.

S-5! will be exhibiting at All Energy Australia, October 28-29, in Melbourne at Stand Q101.

item.title: Construction innovations could cut gigawatt-scale solar costs by 22%
item.dc:creator: Patrick Jowett
item.description: Research from Lightsource bp finds combining automated foundation piling, steel-frame solar panels, bolt-free solar module installations and on-site pre-assembly could also reduce installation time of gigawatt-sized solar farms by up to 30%.
item.content:encoded:
The construction of gigawatt-sized solar farms could be transformed by adopting four technical innovations, according to research by Lightsource bp.

The UK-headquartered independent power producer (IPP) has shared findings from the investigation phase of its NextGen Solar Programme, which is reviewing how gigwatt-scale solar farms are built.

The programme is exploring how four areas of innovation – automated foundation piling, a frameless panel design that uses steel rather than aluminium, press-fit bolt-free module installations, and on-site pre-assembly – can reduce the costs and time required to construct gigawatt-sized solar farms.

Results from the initial investigation found combining these four construction innovations could cut direct installation costs by around 22% and reduce installation time by up to 30%, when compared with current standard practice.

Chris Buckland, Global Technical Director of Lightsource bp, told pv magazine the analysis is based on assessment of “newly-developed solar industry offerings from China, Europe and Northern America, with a focus on automation and novel installation method.”

Buckland added that a construction approach combining the four innovations is intended for large-scale PV development from 2028 onwards.

“It remains at the development stage but is expected to become relevant to major projects over the next three years,” he explained. “We plan to run trials in Australia and the United States to validate supplier data points and support technical assessment and bankability, with initial results targeted within the next 18 months.”

Lightsource bp’s analysis says automated piling rigs that use GPS precision can reduce installation time by up to 12.5%. Automated piling replaces manual pile driving, it adds, in turn lowering costs and improving consistency while also potentially reducing the risk of injury to site workers.

Additional analysis by the IPP says a press-fit, bolt-free solar module installation that enables solar panels to click into position has the potential to reduce installation time by up to 30% when combined with automated piling and a new module design.

“The solution aims to simplify module installation by replacing conventional clamps and bolts, delivering potential savings through reduced installation time and balance-of-system costs,” Buckland told pv magazine.

“We are also exploring replacing aluminium frames with steel options. Due to confidentiality requirements, we cannot provide the cost assessments.”

An additional statement from Lightsource bp explains its NextGen Solar Programme now moves from modelling and analysis into real-world validation, with trials on active projects including automated piling systems, robotic module placement and advanced cable harnessing solutions to verify cost, time and safety assumptions.

“We know that demand for solar energy is rising, and building for gigawatt scale is constrained by existing construction methods, impacting some projects commercial viability,” Buckland explained.

“The NextGen Solar Programme has delivered a practical, evidenced-based roadmap for scaling solar farm construction efficiently, and we are now moving to validate these solutions under real operating conditions.”

From pv magazine Global
